name: Substance
statement: The fundamental things that exist in their own right and bear properties, rather than being had by anything.
statementAccent: exist in their own right and bear properties
meaning: Substance is one of the most central and contested notions in metaphysics. Broadly, a substance is a fundamental entity, a basic thing that exists in its own right and is the bearer of properties and the subject of predication and change, as opposed to the properties, qualities, or modes that depend on it and are had by it. Substances are the relatively independent, fundamental items of an ontology, individual things like a particular horse, a person, or a rock; properties, by contrast, cannot subsist on their own but require a substance to belong to. The notion descends from Aristotle, whose Categories treats the individual thing, this man or this horse, as primary substance, that which is neither said of nor present in a subject, a subject that bears properties but is not itself a property of anything, while species and genera such as man or animal are secondary substances; in the Metaphysics Aristotle asks what the substance, or ousia, of a thing is, considering matter, form, and the compound, and favors form or essence. A major modern debate concerns the internal structure of an individual substance: substratum or bare-particular theory, associated with Locke's something, I know not what that supports qualities, holds that a substance is a propertyless substratum bearing its properties, while bundle theory, associated with Hume and Russell, denies any substratum and takes an object to be just a bundle of its co-present properties. Descartes, Spinoza, and Leibniz gave substance central and differing roles, and empiricists such as Hume criticized it.
mechanism: The concept of substance does its work by marking a fundamental division in what there is, between the things that exist independently and bear properties and the properties, modes, or qualities that depend on them. A property like redness or a mode like a particular shape does not float free; it is always the redness or shape of some thing, and that thing, the substance, is what has the properties and persists as their subject. Aristotle's Categories fixes this by defining primary substance as what is neither said of a subject, as a species is said of an individual, nor present in a subject, as a quality is present in a thing; the individual is the ultimate subject of predication and the bearer of qualities, a this, and it can persist through change while remaining numerically one and the same, receiving contrary qualities at different times. In the Metaphysics Aristotle deepens the inquiry, asking what the substance of a thing really is and arguing that its form or essence, rather than its matter or the compound, is primary substance. The modern debate turns to the constitution of an individual substance. Substratum theory answers that beneath a thing's properties lies a bare bearer that has them but is not itself any of them, Locke's unknown support standing under the qualities; bundle theory answers that there is no such bare substrate, and that the object simply is the collection of its compresent properties, nothing more. Alongside this runs the criterion of independence: substances are often characterized as ontologically independent, able to exist on their own, whereas properties and modes cannot exist without a substance, and it is this criterion that Descartes, Spinoza, and Leibniz variously deploy in their systems.

examples.text: For Aristotle the individual thing, this man or this horse, is primary substance, neither said of nor present in a subject.
Substratum theory posits a bare bearer of properties; bundle theory says an object just is a bundle of its properties.
Substances are often marked by ontological independence, existing on their own, while properties cannot exist without them.

variants.name: Substratum theory
variants.text: The view, associated with Locke, that a substance is a propertyless substratum, an unknown support, bearing its properties.

variants.name: Bundle theory
variants.text: The view, associated with Hume and Russell, that an object is nothing but a bundle of its compresent properties.

whyItMatters: Substance is a foundational and enduring concept in metaphysics, organizing our thinking about what fundamentally exists. The distinction between substances and their properties, between the independent bearers of qualities and the qualities they bear, structures ontology and underlies our ordinary conception of a world of persisting things that have features and undergo change. Aristotle's analysis of substance in the Categories and Metaphysics set the agenda for two millennia and remains a touchstone, and the notion was central to the great systems of early modern philosophy: Descartes defined substance as what depends on nothing else to exist and built his dualism of thinking and extended substance on it, Spinoza concluded there is only one substance, God or Nature, of which all else is a mode, and Leibniz populated reality with infinitely many simple substances, the monads. The modern debate between substratum and bundle theories continues to probe what an individual thing is, and empiricist criticism, from Hume onward, of the idea of a bare, unknowable support keeps the concept under pressure. Questions of substance bear directly on persistence, on the metaphysics of objects, and on the substance-attribute distinction throughout philosophy.

working.text: distinguish the fundamental things that exist in their own right from the properties they bear.
identify substances as the ultimate subjects of predication that persist through change and depend on nothing else.
ask whether a substance is a bare substratum bearing properties or just a bundle of properties.

limits: The concept of substance is fundamental but deeply contested, and each way of developing it faces objections. Substratum theory is charged with positing a mysterious, propertyless bearer that we could never encounter or characterize, Locke's own something, I know not what, which empiricists from Hume onward attacked as an unknowable posit doing no real explanatory work. Bundle theory avoids the bare substratum but must explain what unifies a bundle into a single object and holds its properties together, and it faces the objection that two distinct things could share all their properties, apparently violating the identity of indiscernibles. The independence criterion for substance is itself problematic, since, as Leibniz objected, a substance cannot exist without its own attributes, so strict independence is hard to state, and refined versions have been proposed. Aristotle's own account is intricate and disputed, and the mark that substance can receive contrary qualities while remaining numerically one, though genuinely his, is drawn from the primary texts rather than restated in every summary. Descartes's strict independence criterion arguably applies fully only to God.
misreadings: Substance in the metaphysical sense is not a kind of stuff or material, like a chemical substance; it is the fundamental thing that bears properties, whatever its matter. It is not obviously a bare substratum, since bundle theorists deny any propertyless bearer and identify the object with its properties. And the independence that marks substance is not easy to state strictly, since substances still depend on having some properties, so treating substance as a material, as necessarily a bare substratum, or as wholly independent of all else, misreads the notion.
origin: The central metaphysical notion, from Aristotle's Categories and Metaphysics and the systems of Descartes, Spinoza, and Leibniz, of a fundamental entity that exists in its own right and bears properties, with rival substratum and bundle accounts of its structure.
